title: Samsung's Lee Jae-yong meets Sam Altman at OpenAI HQ in San Francisco
subtitle: The meeting followed a July push by Samsung to lock in HBM supply and foundry work tied to OpenAI's 750 GW-scale compute plan through 2030.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Lee Jae-yong met with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman at OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters on July 25. Neither company disclosed the agenda, but the timing lines up with two threads already in motion: Samsung's push to secure long-term high-bandwidth-memory (HBM) commitments as HBM4 volumes ramp, and OpenAI's public July 24 commitment to a $750 billion, 10-year buildout of compute infrastructure through 2030. Korean press reporting also raised advanced foundry manufacturing and Samsung's internal generative-AI transformation as likely topics.

For Samsung, the meeting matters because HBM is now the pricing pin holding the AI accelerator market together. Nvidia, AMD, and every custom-silicon program at a hyperscaler compete for the same HBM supply, and Samsung has spent the last year fighting to close the gap with SK Hynix on both HBM3E and HBM4 qualification volumes. A direct commitment framework with a single hyperscale buyer — the way SK Hynix has locked in slots with Nvidia — would give Samsung memory the visibility it needs for capex planning through 2028. For OpenAI, memory supply is now the binding constraint on the 2027-2028 slice of its 750 GW plan, not GPU count or power.

The foundry question is the harder one. OpenAI has said publicly that it wants a diversified manufacturing base for the custom silicon it is co-designing with Broadcom, and TSMC's advanced nodes are booked out. Samsung Foundry's 2nm process is the only credible non-TSMC option at the leading edge, but its historical yield gap has kept the top AI silicon designers away. A meeting at this level is not a manufacturing commitment, but it is where the multi-year conversations that lead to one begin — and if Samsung Foundry lands even one flagship AI customer for a 2nm design, the competitive picture in leading-edge foundry changes materially.

For learners: pay attention to when CEOs and chairs fly to see each other in person. In an industry that runs on Slack and Zoom, an in-person visit at this altitude usually signals a supply relationship that both sides want on more than a purchase order — the kind that requires multi-year capacity carve-outs, joint roadmap sharing, or co-investment in fab capacity. You will rarely see the deal disclosed at the meeting; you will see the memo of understanding a quarter or two later. Watch Samsung's next capex guidance and OpenAI's next infrastructure announcement — that is where whatever came out of this meeting will actually show up.
